newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil church warns of rising land violence.
newsitem.headline: Brazil church warns of rising land violence.

text.p: A Catholic Church group in Brazil said on Friday 112 people have been killed in conflicts over land ownership since President Fernando Henrique Cardoso took office in 1995 and levels of violence could rise.
"The numbers do not lie," said an annual report by the church's Pastoral Land Commission (CPT), a strident critic of the government's handling of the explosive land reform issue.

In 1995 and 1996, the first two year's of Cardoso's term, 1.3 million people were involved in 1,304 separate conflicts over land, mining rights and labour issues in Brazil's vast and often lawless interior, the report said.

So far in 1997 17 landless and small plot farmers have died in clashes, taking the total since 1995 to 112. "If this rhythm continues we are heading for similar levels of violence to the 1980s when conflict was at its worst," it said.
It also said that while 976 people died in land disputes between 1985 and 1996 only seven people were convicted of ordering the killings and two of them are on the run.

Cardoso has repeatedly said his programme to settle 280,000 families in four years is the most ambitious ever undertaken in Brazil and represents a big step toward addressing the country's acute land ownership imbalance. About 50 percent of arable land belongs to just two percent of landowners.
But the CPT dismissed Cardoso's land reform programme as "propaganda" and said it fell "millions of people and hectares short" of meeting the needs of Brazil's rural poor.

The radical Landless Movement, which works closely with the CPT, says up to 4.8 million Brazilian families need land. Many of those people have already been forced to migrate into urban shantytowns or work as rural labourers.
The CPT report detailed 750 conflicts in the countryside in 1996, the highest number since 1988. Of those, 653 involved disputes over land ownership, 32.6 percent up on 1995.

The number of people involved in the land disputes in 1996 rose 33.8 percent to 481,490 while the amount of land at issue rose just 4.2 percent to 3.4 million hectares, showing a sharp increase in demands for settlement, the report said.
The CPT also found an increase in the number of expulsion orders issued by Brazilian courts to landowners seeking to clear landless settlers from their farms.
